claims.text: All compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are equiatomic, single-phase FCC materials produced by standardized thermomechanical processing.
Additional elemental interactions in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni promote a unique local chemical short-range order relative to its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Local chemical short-range order alters the spatial distribution of stacking-fault energies.
Variations in local chemical short-range order produce spatial fluctuations in lattice distortion.
Spatial fluctuations in stacking-fault energy and lattice distortion modulate dislocation mobility and deformation mechanisms.
The full complement of elements in the quinary alloy fosters local atomic clustering.
Local atomic clustering in the quinary alloy creates a non-uniform stacking-fault-energy landscape.
The non-uniform stacking-fault-energy landscape promotes dislocation interactions including cross-slip and deformation twinning.
The promoted dislocation interactions enhance work hardening and ductility.
Diverse local chemical ordering is absent or diminished in the reduced-complexity quaternary and ternary alloys.
Reduced local ordering in the quaternary and ternary alloys interrupts dislocation motion less effectively and produces different deformation behavior.
Under identical room-temperature tensile conditions, the quinary alloy will have higher work-hardening rates than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Under identical room-temperature tensile conditions, the quinary alloy will exhibit delayed plastic instability relative to its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Under identical room-temperature tensile conditions, the quinary alloy will have greater ductility than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The controlled comparison applies the same strain rate, temperature, environment, and sample preparation to all compositions.
The hypothesis is restricted to equiatomic, single-phase FCC alloys processed by similar thermomechanical routes and tested in conventional room-temperature tension.
The hypothesis would be falsified if the quinary alloy lacks statistically significant work-hardening or ductility enhancement relative to the reduced-component alloys.
The hypothesis would also be falsified if local chemical order and stacking-fault-energy distributions are similar across the compared compositions.
